record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: Can one compute a mapping f: Σ* -> Σ* and a constant c > 1 such that for every word w with square density rho_sq(w) >= 1, the image f(w) satisfies rho_sq(f(w)) >= c rho_sq(w)?

evidence.quote: Can we compute a mapping f : Σ*-→ Σ* for which a constant c > 1 exists such that, for all win Σ*, if rhosq(w)>= 1 then we have rhosq( f (w))>= crhosq(w)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet with |Σ| ≥ 2 and let Σ* denote the set of finite words over Σ. For a word w ∈ Σ*, a square is a nonempty factor of the form uu (with u ∈ Σ⁺); let s(w) denote the number of distinct squares occurring as factors of w. Define the square density of w by
  ρ_sq(w) = s(w) / |w|       (with ρ_sq(ε) := 0).

Question: Does there exist a computable mapping f : Σ* → Σ* and a constant c > 1 such that, for every word w ∈ Σ* satisfying ρ_sq(w) ≥ 1, one has
  ρ_sq(f(w)) ≥ c · ρ_sq(w)?
artifact.status_search_result: Searches surface related work on constructing words with high distinct square densities (e.g., constructions approaching density 5/6 and sequences of FS-double squares whose square density tends to 1), but no source explicitly resolves the existence of a computable amplification map f with multiplicative factor c > 1 acting on words of square density ≥ 1. Status appears unresolved in the literature retrieved.

status_evidence.title: Constructing Words with High Distinct Square Densities
status_evidence.snippet: Constructions of words whose distinct-square density approaches 5/6.
status_evidence.claim: Related work studies high distinct-square densities but does not establish the desired amplification mapping.

status_evidence.title: The square density of words having a sequence of FS-double squares
status_evidence.snippet: The square density of constructed words converges to 1.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work addresses limiting square density but not a uniform multiplicative amplification by a constant c>1.
